title: Stare decisis after a change in interpretive method
shortTitle: Stare decisis after a change in interpretive method
summary: Stare decisis governs continued adherence to prior decisions. Loper Bright distinguishes rejection of Chevron’s method from reopening every earlier holding that upheld a particular agency action.
notes:
The majority says that earlier agency-action holdings, including Chevron’s Clean Air Act holding, remain subject to statutory stare decisis. Their use of Chevron alone does not supply the special justification needed to overrule them. At the same time, the Court overrules the general interpretive framework on grounds of poor statutory reasoning, unworkability, and unreliable or destabilizing reliance. Kagan argues for stronger adherence because Congress can correct statutory decisions and actors operated against the framework for decades. (Printed 951–960.)

The notes identify a difficult question about the content of an earlier holding. Brand X distinguished a judicial finding of one permissible reading from a finding that a statute has only one allowable meaning. After Loper Bright, a court’s best reading might differ from the agency interpretation previously upheld as permissible. Whether and how the older holding controls requires analysis; the text does not resolve every possible configuration. A graph link between these accounts represents that tension, rather than an instruction to treat all Chevron-era precedents as erased. (Printed 936–937, 966.)

Kisor provides a comparison. Its five-Justice stare decisis discussion retained a long series of regulatory-interpretation precedents and emphasized settled regulatory constructions. The different outcomes in Kisor and Loper Bright should be assessed through the stated considerations and the source being interpreted, while preserving the disputes among the Justices over the significance of history, workability, and reliance. (Printed 994–1001.)
